input: When evaluating whether a solar array represents a worthwhile investment, it is essential to consider the time value of money, and a capital appraisal based on discounted cash flow provides a robust framework for doing so. In this case, the installed cost of the array is $651k, while the expected net saving is estimated at $125k per year over a period of 10 years. By applying a discount rate of 8%, the present value of these anticipated savings is calculated to be $839k, resulting in a net present value of $188k. This positive figure suggests that, on the basis of the estimates used, the project more than recovers its initial outlay in discounted terms. However, it is crucial to bear in mind that the savings figures are derived from vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. Consequently, while the appraisal appears favourable, the outcome in practice will depend heavily on whether the estimated savings are actually realised, highlighting the importance of careful monitoring following installation. Nevertheless, decision-makers should be aware that appraisals of this kind are only as reliable as the assumptions that underpin them, and sensitivity to the discount rate and to the saving estimate is an inherent feature of the method rather than a defect in its application here.
target: Installation of the solar array returns a net present value of $188k at a discount rate of 8%. The appraisal sets an installed cost of $651k against an expected net saving of $125k per year over 10 years. Discounted over the appraisal horizon, the savings have a present value of $839k, and the excess of that value over the installed cost is the net present value stated above. The appraisal is a comparison of two quantities on one basis: the cost is a quotation, incurred at installation, while the savings are a stream spread over the horizon and discounted back to the same point in time. The saving is the load-bearing figure in the appraisal, and it is also the least secure: the savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. The net present value is therefore a property of the estimates, not of the installation. Metered savings after installation are what would convert the estimate into evidence, and the appraisal stands open to revision until they exist. A measured saving below the estimate would lower the present value year by year, and a shortfall early in the horizon weighs more heavily than the same shortfall late in it, because discounting shrinks the later years more.
